items.title: Religion should be removed from terrorism definition under Australian law as it gives ‘false credibility’, watchdog says
items.summary:
Independent National Security Legislation Monitor says reference to religion has ‘contributed to discrimination and violence against religious minorities’

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Religion should be removed from Australia’s terrorism definition and making bomb threats should not result in life imprisonment, the country’s national security laws watchdog has said.

The highly anticipated report from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor (INSLM), released Thursday, reviewed how terrorism has been defined in Australia over the past 25 years after a suite of laws were introduced following the September 11 attacks in the United States.

Continue reading...
items.t: Religion should be removed from terrorism definition under Australian law as it gives ‘false credibility’, watchdog says

items.title: US warned supplying nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish its own fleet for ‘many years’
items.summary:
Congressional Budget Office also questions whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into a conflict with China under Aukus deal

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Providing nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US navy’s own fleet for “many years”, a new report for the US Congress has cautioned, questioning whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into service in a conflict with China.

The US navy’s latest shipbuilding plan does not countenance the Aukus agreement in its forecasts at all, noting only in a footnote that the transfer of any Virginia-class submarine to Australia “has not been factored into the plan”, the report says.

Continue reading...
items.t: US warned supplying nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish its own fleet for ‘many years’

items.title: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message
items.summary:
Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.

Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.

Continue reading...
items.t: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message

items.title: Howard-era minister Sharman Stone dies via voluntary assisted dying, aged 75
items.summary:
The former Liberal MP had fought a long battle against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer

  • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone has died via voluntary assisted dying after spending much of her political career advocating that people should have autonomy over their bodies.

Stone died aged 75 on Wednesday surrounded by family after a long fight against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. She had a long political career, serving as the minister for workforce participation from 2006-07 and the ambassador for women and girls from 2016-20.

Continue reading...
items.t: Howard-era minister Sharman Stone dies via voluntary assisted dying, aged 75

items.title: Major anti-gang offensive in Haiti kills 34 suspected gang members
items.summary: Haitian security forces launched a major offensive on Thursday to retake Martissant, a strategic corridor linking Port-au-Prince with the country's western and southern regions that gangs have controlled for five years. Police said at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in clashes involving a private security task force.
items.t: Major anti-gang offensive in Haiti kills 34 suspected gang members

items.title: Anthropic goes public after blockbuster IPO but fails to revive AI trade
items.summary: Anthropic has become the first pure-play AI developer to be publicly traded on the stock market, following a record-setting IPO. The stock opened 34% higher, briefly valuing the company at more than $2 trillion, before ending its first day of trading up 17%. However, Wall Street indexes closed sharply lower as investors took profits, reflecting underlying market jitters about the AI trade.
items.t: Anthropic goes public after blockbuster IPO but fails to revive AI trade

items.title: Mark Speakman resigns and says Liberals face ‘existential threat’ as NSW exodus continues
items.summary:
Former NSW opposition leader warns party against becoming ‘Labor lite’ or ‘One Nation lite’ in late-night speech

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Former New South Wales opposition leader Mark Speakman will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

Continue reading...
items.t: Mark Speakman resigns and says Liberals face ‘existential threat’ as NSW exodus continues

items.title: French far-left candidate Mélenchon opens door to alliance with rival Greens candidate
items.summary: French far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon opened the door to an alliance with France's Greens on Thursday after their presidential candidate Marine Tondelier said she was ready to "work on a coalition around" the veteran leftist. Tondelier's overture has further boosted Mélenchon's campaign for the Élysée Palace – and angered moderates on the centre-left.
items.t: French far-left candidate Mélenchon opens door to alliance with rival Greens candidate

items.title: Kenyan marathon champion banned for doping
items.summary: In tonight's edition, Kenyan athletics superstar and reigning marathon world champion Peres Jepchirchir is banned for three years for doping. Also, South African judges leave the courtroom behind and tour a repatriation centre before handing down judgment in 33 emergency asylum applications. And Ghana's presidency has a new jet, but critics of the ruling party are not on board.
items.t: Kenyan marathon champion banned for doping

items.title: Russian strikes on Kyiv kill one, damage Dutch and Austrian embassies
items.summary: A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged a historic cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands. Loud explosions erupted across the Ukraine capital throughout the day as the leaders of Russia, China and the United States held a historic meeting in China that put Russia's President Vladimir Putin in international spotlight. FRANCE 24's Laurent Berstecher reports.
items.t: Russian strikes on Kyiv kill one, damage Dutch and Austrian embassies

items.title: 'We're seeing in real time the effects that AI is going to have on cybersecurity', expert says
items.summary: FRANCE 24's Monte Francis speaks with Dr. R. David Edelman, Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, also former Director for Cybersecurity on the National Security Council under the Obama administration. He explains that the latest spate of network outages shows "in real time the effects that AI is going to have on cybersecurity" adding that "the one thing that's tying most of these outages together is that companies and institutions are racing to patch a system that's been identified as vulnerable, and they're patching what themselves are pretty creaky digital systems".
items.t: 'We're seeing in real time the effects that AI is going to have on cybersecurity', expert says

items.title: 'Humanitarian mission' for Kostiantynivka: Is it a trap?
items.summary: Russian President Putin has proposed an evacuation of the Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka, like the recent operation in Oleshky. Experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?
items.t: 'Humanitarian mission' for Kostiantynivka: Is it a trap?

items.title: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches
items.summary:
Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire

British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.

It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that EU students would pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line.

Continue reading...
items.t: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches

items.title: Kushner says Trump 'open' to extend NATO mutual defense-type clause to Ukraine
items.summary: US envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday that President Donald Trump was open to extending to Ukraine a security guarantee similar to NATO's mutual defense clause, but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests too. The comments came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz qualified the summit between the presidents of the United States, Russia and China as a "photo op". FRANCE 24's international affairs commentator Douglas Herbert explains.
items.t: Kushner says Trump 'open' to extend NATO mutual defense-type clause to Ukraine

items.title: Macron urges Ukraine's allies to 'reopen the question' of NATO membership
items.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called for Ukraine's allies to speed up the delivery of urgently needed air defence systems and urged them to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's NATO membership after talks in Berlin aimed at reaffirming European support for Kyiv.
items.t: Macron urges Ukraine's allies to 'reopen the question' of NATO membership

items.title: Iran may be working on biological weapons, Trump says
items.summary: President Trump told Fox News there are indications Iran may be working on biological or chemical weapons as the war drags on toward its ninth month.
items.t: Iran ramps up retaliation on Gulf countries after U.S. strikes

items.title: A president among body bags: Photo ops spark outrage in Colombia
items.summary: Since taking office in August, Colombia's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella has regularly posted videos that show him walking among body bags supposedly holding the remains of rebel fighters – a communications strategy that has sparked widespread criticism.
items.t: A president among body bags: Photo ops spark outrage in Colombia

items.title: Three of a kind? Xi hosts Trump and Putin as Ukraine war grinds on
items.summary: Gang of three or glorified photo op? Xi Jinping hosting Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Already, our Monday panel rejected attempts to paint the three-way meeting as a new Yalta, as in the 1945 sit-down on the Black Sea that defined the post-war security architecture of Europe.
items.t: Three of a kind? Xi hosts Trump and Putin as Ukraine war grinds on

items.title: Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral meeting: Trump's recognition of China and Russia as 'peers of the US'
items.summary: Genie Godula is pleased to welcome Olivia Cheung. The trilateral meeting between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit was significant despite the absence of concrete agreements, according to Cheung. “The significance is seen in the precedence of the United States seeing and giving recognition that China and Russia are peers of the United States,” she explained, adding that “the image of a G3 is very significant.”
items.t: Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral meeting: Trump's recognition of China and Russia as 'peers of the US'

items.title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from record one light-day away, 49 years after launch
items.summary: The Voyager 1 probe launched by NASA nearly a half century ago has reached a distance from Earth of one light day (more than 26 billion kilometres), the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from our planet. The space agency received a signal from the spacecraft Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent.
items.t: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from record one light-day away, 49 years after launch

items.title: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
items.summary:
Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda

The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.

A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.

Continue reading...
items.t: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries

items.title: Iraq's risky standoff: The state vs. Iran-allied militias
items.summary: This week, Iraqi security forces surrounded an area run by the Kataib Hezbollah militia. Onlookers describe it as the most dangerous confrontation between the Iraqi state and Iran-allied militias in decades.
items.t: Iraq's risky standoff: The state vs. Iran-allied militias

items.title: Ukraine allies warn ‘Yalta format’ will not bring about peace – as it happened
items.summary:
Berlin meeting of the ‘coalition of the willing’ comes after Trump declared Putin a ‘friend’ during trilateral meeting with Xi in China

For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media, includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever.

There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues:

“The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.”

Continue reading...

items.title: French media regulator says it will monitor top YouTubers for bias in election coverage
items.summary: Rules designed to safeguard media pluralism during elections campaigns will apply to France's most influential YouTubers in the run-up to next year's presidential contest, media regulator Arcom warned on Thursday, reflecting the growing influence of content creators whose audiences often outstrip those of traditional media companies.
items.t: French media regulator says it will monitor top YouTubers for bias in election coverage

items.summary: The presidents of China, the US and Russia have held an unprecedented summit. While Trump said the three leaders were "making history," Xi described the talks as "fruitful" and Putin called them "open and candid."
items.t: Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have held trilateral talks ― but what did they achieve?

items.summary: Despite warm words between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen Thursday, the simmering trade war between Washington and Beijing still looks to be no closer to resolution.
items.t: What impact will the Shenzhen summit have on the US-China trade war?

items.title: Is Europe now in the shadow of a Trump, Putin and Xi alliance? – podcast
items.summary:
Andy Burnham is meeting western leaders in Berlin and Brussels this week, to discuss Ukraine and closer ties to the EU. Meanwhile, Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have met at the Apec summit in China. Is this the start of a global shift of power away from Europe, or was it just a hyped-up photo opportunity?

You can read Pippa Crerar’s article on the EU’s approach to a reset with the UK here

items.title: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for a rare 3-way meeting in China
items.summary: Russia says Putin, Trump and China's Xi agreed during a rare meeting to boost gas and oil production, and "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war."

items.title: Bangladesh: Hasina supporters vandalise ruling party office
items.summary: Hundreds of supporters of ousted Bangladesh premier Sheikh Hasina staged street protests on Thursday, as a wave of arson attacks escalated tensions ahead of her planned return from exile next month.

items.title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
items.summary:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

Continue reading...
items.t: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars

items.title: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
items.summary:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake

Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.

The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.

Continue reading...
items.t: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China

items.title: US has 'unbalanced approach' on DR Congo deal, Rwanda's foreign minister says
items.summary: In an interview with FRANCE 24, Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe said the Trump administration had "an unbalanced approach" in implementing the DR Congo peace deal it brokered. He also said that the recent row over the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie's top job was "manufactured in Paris and Kinshasa". Finally, he defended a deal for Rwanda to host failed asylum seekers from five European countries.

items.title: 🔴Anthropic soars more than 30% to $2 trillion valuation on first day of trading

items.title: How much do businesses want to pay for AI?
items.summary: Four years after ChatGPT went mainstream, generative AI is transforming how we live and work. It's also been a major driver of economic growth, with massive amounts of money poured into expanding global computing capacity. But now, there are signs of a slowdown in AI spending as companies take a reality check: are they getting sufficient returns on their investments and how much artificial intelligence do they actually need?
items.t: How much do businesses want to pay for AI?

items.title: Inside France's mental health crisis: Are the French all right?
items.summary: This week, we try to get inside the heads of French people, with a deep dive into mental health in France. For a nation that loves analysing its problems, its mental health figures make for sobering reading: nearly one in five French people are affected by a mental health issue.
items.t: Inside France's mental health crisis: Are the French all right?

items.title: ICJ ruling on Myanmar genocide: ‘Historic victory for Rohingya, landmark for international justice’
items.summary: Erin Ogunkeye welcomes Reed Brody, Member of the International Commission of Jurists, Human Rights Lawyer and veteran war crimes prosecutor. The International Court of Justice's ruling on Myanmar marks, according to Brody, "a historic victory for the Rohingya, but also a landmark for international justice." He explains how the court assessed evidence of genocidal intent, rejecting Myanmar's justification of its military operations as counterterrorism. He argues that "the existence of an armed conflict or a security objective doesn't exclude genocidal intent," a finding he believes will have "far-reaching implications in future genocide cases," including South Africa's case against Israel over Gaza. Brody also discusses the Gambia's role in bringing the case and growing challenges to international accountability, warning that "we're in a very dangerous moment."
items.t: ICJ ruling on Myanmar genocide: ‘Historic victory for Rohingya, landmark for international justice’

items.title: Xi demonstrating China's 'global status', occupying 'central position' in relation to Trump & Putin
items.summary: Sharon Gaffney is pleased to welcome Rex Li, professor of international relations at King's College London. For Professor Li, the meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in China is less about "reaching concrete agreements and a common position." Rather, he argues, it is about demonstrating Xi's ability to bring the American and Russian leaders together to discuss major geopolitical issues. Li believes that Xi Jinping has the most to gain from the meeting, as it allows him to demonstrate China's global status and its role as a diplomatic convener. Putin may also benefit from the opportunity to meet the two leaders despite Russia's international isolation following its invasion of Ukraine.
items.t: Xi demonstrating China's 'global status', occupying 'central position' in relation to Trump & Putin

items.title: New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote
items.summary:
Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda

It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘New page in history?’ Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote

items.title: Gender pay gap: French women work "for free” from today
items.summary: Women in Europe are still paid less than men, with the gap falling from 15.1% in 2016 to 11.1% in 2024, according to Eurostat. In France, women symbolically start working for free from 10:51 am on Thursday, 19 November, and at the current pace equality would not be reached until 2062. Experts warn that AI could make things worse by eliminating administrative and legal jobs where many women work, while childbirth and short paternity leave continue to slow women’s careers.
items.t: Gender pay gap: French women work "for free” from today

items.title: 'GTA VI': A masterpiece? Fans react to gaming's biggest release

We also look at U2's new album and tour marking 50 years of the band, discover the French comic book that Pope Leo is reading and meet the women redefining Mexico's Mariachi tradition.
items.t: 'GTA VI': A masterpiece? Fans react to gaming's biggest release

items.title: The chocolate countdown: The art of the advent calendar
items.summary: The holiday season is almost upon us and with it come advent calendars. The annual physical countdown originated in 19th-century Germany as a Christian tradition to count down the days until Christmas. Eugénie Pont from the magazine Fou de Pâtisserie tells us more about what we can expect from the biggest chocolate makers in France.
items.t: The chocolate countdown: The art of the advent calendar

items.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
items.summary:
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

Continue reading...
items.t: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked

items.summary: Iran takes the offensive with attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and airstrikes on several countries around the Persian Gulf.

items.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?

items.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
items.summary:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

Continue reading...
items.t: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns

items.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
items.summary:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Continue reading...
items.t: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN

items.title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
items.summary:
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.

items.title: Apec summit as it happened: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
items.summary:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here

Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday.

It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.

items.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
items.summary:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

items.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
items.summary:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.

Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”

items.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
items.summary:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
